fragments.normalized_text: HTTP Semantics
fragments.text: HTTP Semantics

fragments.normalized_text: The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a stateless application- level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypertext information systems.
fragments.text:
The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a stateless application-
   level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypertext information
   systems.

fragments.normalized_text: This document describes the overall architecture of HTTP, establishes common terminology, and defines aspects of the protocol that are shared by all versions.
fragments.text:
This document describes the overall architecture of HTTP,
   establishes common terminology, and defines aspects of the protocol
   that are shared by all versions.

fragments.normalized_text: In this definition are core protocol elements, extensibility mechanisms, and the "http" and "https" Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.
fragments.text:
In this definition are core
   protocol elements, extensibility mechanisms, and the "http" and
   "https" Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.

fragments.normalized_text: Introduction
fragments.text: Introduction

fragments.normalized_text: The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a family of stateless, application-level, request/response protocols that share a generic interface, extensible semantics, and self-descriptive messages to enable flexible interaction with network-based hypertext information systems.
fragments.text:
The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a family of stateless,
   application-level, request/response protocols that share a generic
   interface, extensible semantics, and self-descriptive messages to
   enable flexible interaction with network-based hypertext information
   systems.

fragments.normalized_text: HTTP hides the details of how a service is implemented by presenting a uniform interface to clients that is independent of the types of resources provided.
fragments.text:
HTTP hides the details of how a service is implemented by presenting
   a uniform interface to clients that is independent of the types of
   resources provided.

fragments.normalized_text: Likewise, servers do not need to be aware of each client's purpose: a request can be considered in isolation rather than being associated with a specific type of client or a predetermined sequence of application steps.
fragments.text:
Likewise, servers do not need to be aware of
   each client's purpose: a request can be considered in isolation
   rather than being associated with a specific type of client or a
   predetermined sequence of application steps.

fragments.normalized_text: This allows general- purpose implementations to be used effectively in many different contexts, reduces interaction complexity, and enables independent evolution over time.
fragments.text:
This allows general-
   purpose implementations to be used effectively in many different
   contexts, reduces interaction complexity, and enables independent
   evolution over time.

fragments.normalized_text: HTTP is also designed for use as an intermediation protocol, wherein proxies and gateways can translate non-HTTP information systems into a more generic interface.
fragments.text:
HTTP is also designed for use as an intermediation protocol, wherein
   proxies and gateways can translate non-HTTP information systems into
   a more generic interface.

fragments.normalized_text: One consequence of this flexibility is that the protocol cannot be defined in terms of what occurs behind the interface.
fragments.text:
One consequence of this flexibility is that the protocol cannot be
   defined in terms of what occurs behind the interface.

fragments.normalized_text: Instead, we are limited to defining the syntax of communication, the intent of received communication, and the expected behavior of recipients.
fragments.text:
Instead, we
   are limited to defining the syntax of communication, the intent of
   received communication, and the expected behavior of recipients.

fragments.normalized_text: If the communication is considered in isolation, then successful actions ought to be reflected in corresponding changes to the observable interface provided by servers.
fragments.text:
If
   the communication is considered in isolation, then successful actions
   ought to be reflected in corresponding changes to the observable
   interface provided by servers.

fragments.normalized_text: However, since multiple clients might act in parallel and perhaps at cross-purposes, we cannot require that such changes be observable beyond the scope of a single response.
fragments.text:
However, since multiple clients might
   act in parallel and perhaps at cross-purposes, we cannot require that
   such changes be observable beyond the scope of a single response.

fragments.normalized_text: History and Evolution
fragments.text: History and Evolution

fragments.normalized_text: HTTP has been the primary information transfer protocol for the World Wide Web since its introduction in 1990.
fragments.text:
HTTP has been the primary information transfer protocol for the World
   Wide Web since its introduction in 1990.

fragments.normalized_text: It began as a trivial mechanism for low-latency requests, with a single method (GET) to request transfer of a presumed hypertext document identified by a given pathname.
fragments.text:
It began as a trivial
   mechanism for low-latency requests, with a single method (GET) to
   request transfer of a presumed hypertext document identified by a
   given pathname.

fragments.normalized_text: As the Web grew, HTTP was extended to enclose requests and responses within messages, transfer arbitrary data formats using MIME-like media types, and route requests through intermediaries.
fragments.text:
As the Web grew, HTTP was extended to enclose
   requests and responses within messages, transfer arbitrary data
   formats using MIME-like media types, and route requests through
   intermediaries.

fragments.normalized_text: These protocols were eventually defined as HTTP/0.9 and HTTP/1.0 (see [HTTP/1.0]).
fragments.text:
These protocols were eventually defined as HTTP/0.9
   and HTTP/1.0 (see [HTTP/1.0]).

fragments.normalized_text: HTTP/1.1 was designed to refine the protocol's features while retaining compatibility with the existing text-based messaging syntax, improving its interoperability, scalability, and robustness across the Internet.
fragments.text:
HTTP/1.1 was designed to refine the protocol's features while
   retaining compatibility with the existing text-based messaging
   syntax, improving its interoperability, scalability, and robustness
   across the Internet.

fragments.normalized_text: This included length-based data delimiters for both fixed and dynamic (chunked) content, a consistent framework for content negotiation, opaque validators for conditional requests, cache controls for better cache consistency, range requests for partial updates, and default persistent connections.
fragments.text:
This included length-based data delimiters for
   both fixed and dynamic (chunked) content, a consistent framework for
   content negotiation, opaque validators for conditional requests,
   cache controls for better cache consistency, range requests for
   partial updates, and default persistent connections.

fragments.normalized_text: HTTP/1.1 was introduced in 1995 and published on the Standards Track in 1997 [RFC2068], revised in 1999 [RFC2616], and revised again in 2014 ([RFC7230] through [RFC7235]).
fragments.text:
HTTP/1.1 was
   introduced in 1995 and published on the Standards Track in 1997
   [RFC2068], revised in 1999 [RFC2616], and revised again in 2014
   ([RFC7230] through [RFC7235]).

fragments.normalized_text: HTTP/2 ([HTTP/2]) introduced a multiplexed session layer on top of the existing TLS and TCP protocols for exchanging concurrent HTTP messages with efficient field compression and server push.
fragments.text:
HTTP/2 ([HTTP/2]) introduced a multiplexed session layer on top of
   the existing TLS and TCP protocols for exchanging concurrent HTTP
   messages with efficient field compression and server push.

fragments.normalized_text: HTTP/3 ([HTTP/3]) provides greater independence for concurrent messages by using QUIC as a secure multiplexed transport over UDP instead of TCP.
fragments.text:
HTTP/3
   ([HTTP/3]) provides greater independence for concurrent messages by
   using QUIC as a secure multiplexed transport over UDP instead of TCP.

fragments.normalized_text: All three major versions of HTTP rely on the semantics defined by this document.
fragments.text:
All three major versions of HTTP rely on the semantics defined by
   this document.

fragments.normalized_text: They have not obsoleted each other because each one has specific benefits and limitations depending on the context of use.
fragments.text:
They have not obsoleted each other because each one
   has specific benefits and limitations depending on the context of
   use.

fragments.normalized_text: Implementations are expected to choose the most appropriate transport and messaging syntax for their particular context.
fragments.text:
Implementations are expected to choose the most appropriate
   transport and messaging syntax for their particular context.

fragments.normalized_text: This revision of HTTP separates the definition of semantics (this document) and caching ([CACHING]) from the current HTTP/1.1 messaging syntax ([HTTP/1.1]) to allow each major protocol version to progress independently while referring to the same core semantics.
fragments.text:
This revision of HTTP separates the definition of semantics (this
   document) and caching ([CACHING]) from the current HTTP/1.1 messaging
   syntax ([HTTP/1.1]) to allow each major protocol version to progress
   independently while referring to the same core semantics.

fragments.normalized_text: Core Semantics
fragments.text: Core Semantics

fragments.normalized_text: HTTP provides a uniform interface for interacting with a resource (Section 3.1) -- regardless of its type, nature, or implementation -- by sending messages that manipulate or transfer representations (Section 3.2).
fragments.text:
HTTP provides a uniform interface for interacting with a resource
   (Section 3.1) -- regardless of its type, nature, or implementation --
   by sending messages that manipulate or transfer representations
   (Section 3.2).

fragments.normalized_text: Each message is either a request or a response.
fragments.text: Each message is either a request or a response.

fragments.normalized_text: A client constructs request messages that communicate its intentions and routes those messages toward an identified origin server.
fragments.text:
A client constructs
   request messages that communicate its intentions and routes those
   messages toward an identified origin server.

fragments.normalized_text: A server listens for requests, parses each message received, interprets the message semantics in relation to the identified target resource, and responds to that request with one or more response messages.
fragments.text:
A server listens for
   requests, parses each message received, interprets the message
   semantics in relation to the identified target resource, and responds
   to that request with one or more response messages.

fragments.normalized_text: The client examines received responses to see if its intentions were carried out, determining what to do next based on the status codes and content received.
fragments.text:
The client
   examines received responses to see if its intentions were carried
   out, determining what to do next based on the status codes and
   content received.

fragments.normalized_text: HTTP semantics include the intentions defined by each request method (Section 9), extensions to those semantics that might be described in request header fields, status codes that describe the response (Section 15), and other control data and resource metadata that might be given in response fields.
fragments.text:
HTTP semantics include the intentions defined by each request method
   (Section 9), extensions to those semantics that might be described in
   request header fields, status codes that describe the response
   (Section 15), and other control data and resource metadata that might
   be given in response fields.

fragments.normalized_text: Semantics also include representation metadata that describe how content is intended to be interpreted by a recipient, request header fields that might influence content selection, and the various selection algorithms that are collectively referred to as "content negotiation" (Section 12).
fragments.text:
Semantics also include representation metadata that describe how
   content is intended to be interpreted by a recipient, request header
   fields that might influence content selection, and the various
   selection algorithms that are collectively referred to as "content
   negotiation" (Section 12).

fragments.normalized_text: HTTP defines a number of generic extension points that can be used to introduce capabilities to the protocol without introducing a new version, including methods, status codes, field names, and further extensibility points within defined fields, such as authentication schemes and cache directives (see Cache-Control extensions in Section 5.2.3 of [CACHING]).

   introduce capabilities to the protocol without introducing a new

   extensibility points within defined fields, such as authentication
   schemes and cache directives (see Cache-Control extensions in
   Section 5.2.3 of [CACHING]).

fragments.normalized_text: Responses are grouped in five classes: Informational responses (100 – 199) Successful responses (200 – 299) Redirection messages (300 – 399) Client error responses (400 – 499) Server error responses (500 – 599) The status codes listed below are defined by RFC 9110.

Informational responses (100 – 199)
Successful responses (200 – 299)
Redirection messages (300 – 399)

Server error responses (500 – 599)
The status codes listed below are defined by RFC 9110.
